title: Participles, active and passive

objectives.can: Recognise the Qal active and passive participles and parse their gender, number and state.

explanation.summary: A Hebrew participle is a verbal adjective. It has gender, number and state like a noun or an adjective, but no person and no tense of its own. It can say that someone is doing something, name 'the one who does it', or work as a noun. The Qal has an active participle, 'doing', and a passive participle, 'done to' or 'having been done'.

sections.heading: The Qal active participle
body: The masculine singular active participle of a strong verb has the shape שֹׁמֵר, 'keeping, a keeper': ō in the first syllable and ē in the second. It is declined like an adjective. The feminine singular adds -ֶת or sometimes -ָה, as in יֹשֶׁבֶת 'a woman sitting'; the masculine plural is שֹׁמְרִים and the feminine plural is -וֹת, as in יֹשְׁבוֹת.

A participle has gender and number but no person. The subject of a clause with a participle is a noun or a pronoun, not something inside the verb: a clause such as 'I am sitting' needs a pronoun like אָנֹכִי, since the participle does not say 'I'. In the word-by-word display a participle has Gender, Number and State, and nothing for Person.

Like a noun, the participle has an absolute and a construct state. In the construct state it is joined closely to what follows: יֹדְעֵי טוֹב וָרָע means 'knowers of good and evil', and שֹׁמְרֵי is 'keepers of'. The ending is shortened as for a noun: שֹׁמְרִים becomes שֹׁמְרֵי.

sections.heading: The Qal passive participle
body: The Qal also has a separate passive participle, with ā in the first syllable and ū in the second: שָׁמוּר 'kept, guarded', כָּתוּב 'written', בָּרוּךְ 'blessed'. It names something that has undergone the action, or the state that results: 'written' means that someone wrote it.

It is declined like an adjective, with feminine -ָה and plural -ִים, -וֹת, and it can be absolute or construct. In the display it has the form label HebForm=passive-participle, kept separate from the active participle. For stems other than the Qal, the passive meaning is carried by other stems (the Niphal, the Pual and the Hophal), which come later in the course.

sections.heading: What a participle does in a sentence
body: As the predicate of a clause, with a subject before or after it, the participle usually presents an action as going on or as a state: אָנֹכִי בֹּרַחַת, 'I am fleeing'. It does not by itself say whether this is past, present or future; the context decides. A participle is often used to describe a present situation or something that is about to happen.

With the article, a participle is 'the one who …': הַהֹלֵךְ 'the one who is walking', 'he who goes'. As an attributive adjective it follows its noun and agrees with it in gender, number and definiteness. And it can be used as a noun without any other word: שֹׁפֵט 'a judge' (literally 'one who judges'), and the participle with a suffix, as in מֹצְאִי 'the one who finds me'.

Because the participle is a verbal adjective, it keeps the verb's grammar. It can have an object, like a verb, and the object may be marked with אֵת, as in Genesis 13:5, where הַהֹלֵךְ is followed by the object marker and the name Abram. Or it stands in the construct state before a noun that is understood as its object: 'knowers of good and evil'.

sections.heading: Telling participles from other words
body: The masculine singular active participle can look like the third masculine singular of the qatal (שֹׁמֵר is not the same as שָׁמַר), but the vowels differ: the participle has ō in the first syllable and ē in the second. A feminine participle ending in -ֶת can look like the infinitive construct of some verbs. Check the vowels and the context.

Some words that have the shape of a participle are listed as nouns, because they are used only as names of persons or things; כֹּהֵן, 'priest', is an example. The corpus lists it as a noun, and a dictionary does too.

misunderstandings: A participle does not have a person or a tense. 'I am fleeing' needs the pronoun אָנֹכִי; whether a participle means 'walks' or 'walked' is decided by the verbs round it.
The passive participle is not an active participle with a different ending. It has its own vowel pattern (ā … ū) and its own meaning: 'written', not 'writing'.
A participle with the article is not a plain adjective. It means 'the one who …' and can stand where a noun stands.
A participle in the construct state is not a verb with a noun after it. It is a noun-like word: 'keepers of the door' is a chain of nouns.

deeper.heading: Participles and the verbal system
body: Some grammarians treat the participle as one of the verb's finite-like forms, because a participle can head a clause by itself, with a subject. Others treat it as a verbal adjective that happens to be used as a predicate. The two descriptions agree on how it is used in the texts: it describes a situation as continuing, or names someone by what he does.
